q: Export markets in the 1980s and 1990s wanted a name they already knew, and one variety duly overtook Pais as Chile's most planted vine. Which?
exp: Cabernet Sauvignon is the backbone of the Chilean trade, from everyday bottlings up to the icons of Alto Maipo. Pais retreated to the old dry-farmed hills of the south.

q: Older Chilean plantings sold as Sauvignon Blanc were found to include a duller, far less aromatic variety. Which?
exp: Sauvignonasse is Friulano, and it gives a broad, mild wine with none of the pungency. Replanting with true Sauvignon Blanc is much of why Chilean whites improved so sharply.

q: Peppery, tightly wound reds from Chile's cool coastal and far northern sites have made the case for which variety?
exp: Syrah from Limari, Elqui and Aconcagua Costa tastes closer to the northern Rhone than to Australia. Carmenere would never finish ripening in any of those places.

q: A Basque immigrant planted a south-west French red near Salto in the 1870s, and Uruguayans called the vine by his name for a century afterwards. Which variety?
exp: Pascual Harriague gave his name to the vine, and Tannat is now Uruguay's flagship. It arrives riper and rounder here than in Madiran, its French home.

q: Most Uruguayan vineyards sit in one department just north of the capital, on clay and limestone near the Rio de la Plata. Which?
exp: Canelones surrounds Montevideo and holds the bulk of the country's planting. Maldonado on the Atlantic coast and Rivera on the Brazilian border are the ambitious newer areas.

q: Humid air off the Atlantic and the Rio de la Plata sets Uruguay's central viticultural problem. What is it?
opts: Drought severe enough to require irrigation everywhere
Fungal disease and rot through the growing season
Too little heat to ripen any red variety
Winter cold that kills vines outright
exp: Canopy management and disciplined spraying matter more here than anywhere else on the continent. Tannat's thick skins are part of why it copes, though its compact bunches still demand careful canopy work and spray penetration.

q: Italian immigrant families settled a humid, hilly zone in Rio Grande do Sul, and its growers have found their strongest suit in one style. Which?
exp: Serra Gaucha takes rain right through the growing season, which suits a lean sparkling base far better than it suits ripe red wine. Vale dos Vinhedos within it was the first Brazilian area granted a geographical indication.

q: Vines planted near the ninth parallel south never go properly dormant, so growers there can take more than one crop a year. Which Brazilian region?
exp: Irrigation from the Sao Francisco river lets the grower decide when to prune and therefore when to pick. It is one of very few places on earth where a vineyard runs on a tropical rather than a seasonal calendar.

q: A Chilean label naming a variety, a vintage and a valley must draw at least what proportion of the wine from each?
exp: Seventy-five percent is the domestic minimum, while wine bound for the European Union has to meet a stricter eighty-five. Most producers work comfortably above either figure.

q: Overhead canopies of wire on high posts, with the fruit hanging in shade beneath, are the traditional Argentine training system. What is it called?
exp: Parral suits table grapes and high-yielding Criolla, and it shelters fruit from a fierce sun. Quality plantings have largely moved to vertical trellising for better exposure and airflow.

q: Argentina has phylloxera in its soils, yet most of its vines are still ungrafted. Which explanation is the accepted one?
opts: Sandy soils and flood irrigation keep the insect's damage in check
The Andes stop the insect from crossing into the country
Winter cold kills the insect off every year
Argentine vines are American hybrids the insect cannot feed on
exp: Phylloxera struggles in sand and fares badly under periodic flooding, and both are ordinary conditions in Mendoza. Chile's position is different again, since the pest never arrived there at all.

q: Flood channels fed the rows for generations, but newer high-altitude plantings in the Uco Valley mostly use what instead?
exp: Drip gives precise control over how much water each vine receives and when, which is the main lever on vigour in a desert. It also works on stony slopes where a flood channel could never be run level.

q: Two Spanish regions alone hold the country's top appellation tier. Rioja is one; which is the other?
exp: Rioja was raised to Denominacion de Origen Calificada in 1991 and Priorat followed, printing the Catalan form DOQ on its labels. The tier demands a long record as an ordinary DO before it can even be applied for.

q: A single estate can carry its own denomination in Spain, ranked above the DO that surrounds it. What is that category called?
opts: Vino de Calidad con Indicacion Geografica
exp: A Vino de Pago recognises one property with a distinct terroir, and the estate must grow and vinify its own fruit. Dominio de Valdepusa in Toledo was the first to be granted it.

q: A region must normally spend years at an intermediate quality level before it may apply for full DO status. Which level is that?
opts: Vino de Calidad con Indicacion Geografica
exp: Five years as a Vino de Calidad before applying for DO, then ten years as a DO before applying for the tier above. The ladder is deliberately slow, so a name has to be earned across decades.

q: Which term on a Spanish label matches what the rest of Europe calls a protected geographical indication?
exp: Vino de la Tierra covers a wide zone with looser rules on grapes and yields. It is often where an ambitious estate goes when it wants to plant something the local DO forbids.
